extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed citizens interested in constitutional theory and the design of republican government
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and judge constitutional arrangements and policies to preserve liberty and prevent arbitrary or monarchic power, focusing on separation/mixing of powers, public education, and institutional safeguards. The guidance is aimed at assessing what structural features make a commonwealth stable and free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of three branches
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance of three branches is alone adequate to restrain the natural tendency toward kingly power; mixing the powers of the one, the few, and the many in equal proportions prevents any single interest of monarchy from prevailing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues repeatedly that a proper mixture (legislative, executive, judicial) in roughly equal proportions is necessary because human nature will continually tend toward concentration of power; only the triple division can decide contest for 'first man' and keep the state ordered. Examples: Spartan and Roman mixtures restrained kingly power for a time but were imperfect because the mixture was not equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate legislative, executive, and judicial powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative and executive (and judicial) powers should be lodged in distinct hands; permitting them to rest in one person or body leaves the people without remedy and invites arbitrary rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If law-makers are also permanent administrators and dispensers of law and justice, there is no appeal against them. Historical evidence (kings who combined making and execution of laws) shows unlimited arbitrary power grew as both functions came into the same hands. Separation ensures governors are accountable to law-makers and prevents usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent passage of tyranny between forms of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against the transfer or transformation of arbitrary/monarchic power from one formal regime into another during political change or reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'interest of monarchy' can reside in a consul, dictator, many, or one; it has lurked under every form. Reforms must take care to prevent tyranny from passing 'out of one form into another' — e.g., standing senates, decemviri, triumvirs, or extended commands that replicate kingly power under new names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creation or maintenance of standing permanent powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing or permanent institutions of concentrated power (standing senate, decemviri, etc.) become instruments of division and arbitrary rule rather than safeguards of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: the standing power of the Roman senate and decemviri became as much levellers/tyrants as kings; standing magistrates often entrench privilege and lead to despotism. Institutional permanence without proper checks invites the same abuses as monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not lengthen commands or terms of office
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening terms of office or military commands creates opportunities for monarchic interest to take root and for officers to accumulate unchecked authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that extending commands in armies or lengthening dictatorships (e.g., Sulla, Caesar) allowed monarchic power to 'creep in' and eventually become permanent. Short, revolving terms and accountable deputies limit this danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent concentration of legislative and executive power in the same hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifically avoid vesting both the law-making and the constant administration/execution of laws in the same person(s), because that combination undermines appeals and remedies for injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where law-makers also execute laws, the people have no recourse; historical kingdoms became absolute when making and executing laws were brought into the same hands. The safety of the state depends on distinct channels for the flow of these powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional checks: appoint different orders to watch one another and give alarm
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitute different offices/orders whose interest it is, in turn, to appeal to the people and to warn of danger, keeping the public constantly vigilant and preventing any one part from usurping power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions so each branch can 'appeal to the people' and thus be self-interested in preserving the laws; this creates continual mutual surveillance and alarm. Without such institutional alarms the people's vigilance cannot be assumed to remain sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government as enabler of transparency and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a mixed (compound) government can bear free communication of truth to the people and compel officials to disclose information necessary for liberty; single assemblies or concentrated executives permit concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority in a single assembly can conceal almost anything from the minority; the crown cannot conceal things from a house of representatives that it ought to know. Mixed government structures (separate branches) help ensure information flows to the public and enable effective oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate the entire populace in the means of preserving liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the people informed of the ways and means essential to preserve their liberty; provide education widely (not only for elites) so that citizens understand political and civil duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer urges public schools, academies, universities, the press, the bar, pulpit, and parliament to be used for instructing all ranks of people; universal education would reduce superstition, knavery, and implicit faith, and increase public opinion that shames tyranny. Education of every class is a political instrument against oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject governance by 'reason of state' in favor of strict honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept 'reason of state' (rafty kingcraft and princely expedience) as justification for regulation of affairs; rule by strict rule of honesty is the safeguard of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders often invoke 'reason of state' to justify tyranny over minorities and eventually over their own party; especially in democracies such pretexts enable oppression. Public policy should be guided by honesty and transparent rules, not by concealed statecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid placing executive power directly into hands of the people or their representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting executive power into the hands of the people, their representatives, or the senate is dangerous because it tempts corruption and gives more opportunity to conceal knavery; it effectively 'bribes' people to betray their own interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that exercising supreme power requires appointing different orders to watch one another; if the people directly hold executive power (or their reps do), they will be distracted by office-seeking, neglect their legislative responsibilities, and enable democratic despotism (triumvirs, decemvirs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor founders and institutional memory to block monarchic tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a reverent public respect for founders of free states and their declarations as a bulwark against the re-emergence of arbitrary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests that declaring in favor of due and orderly succession in supreme assemblies and venerating founders helps 'block up the way against monarchic tyranny' by making clear public standards for liberty and succession; institutional memory reinforces norms that prevent usurpation.
